%

%
%   (B) "What a Single-Horizon Comparison Cannot See: Exposure Concentration in
%        a Learned-Ranker Matching Market, and How Long It Lasts"
%
%   (C) "How Long Does a Recommender's Exposure Gap Last? A Three-Hundred-Epoch
%        Test in a Simulated Matching Market"
%
% Set in the document: (B). It names the methodological claim, which is the one
% the paper establishes, and promises nothing about mechanism.
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\title{What a Single-Horizon Comparison Cannot See:\\
       Exposure Concentration in a Learned-Ranker Matching Market,\\
       and How Long It Lasts}

\author{}
\date{}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent
A recommender that decides which candidates a matching market's agents ever see
changes what a preference list means. This paper shows that measuring the harm at
one horizon can invert the conclusion. In a simulated market of 1000 agents whose
top-20 shortlists come from a neural collaborative filter, exposure Gini under the
learned ranker exceeds an oracle's by $\gapBaseTwenty$ $[\gapBaseTwentyLo,
\gapBaseTwentyHi]$ at a hundred epochs over twenty seeds, and is positive on all
twenty of a fresh seed set. Extending to three hundred shows no floor: the gap peaks at $\gapPeak$, and a
pre-declared equivalence test at a $0.002$ margin puts the tail inside it, so the
hundred-epoch number describes a transient rather than a bias, though a flat tail
is also what a very slow decay looks like. The ordering survives all
\nSweepCells{} sweep cells but varies fivefold in size, and the mechanism usually
offered for the decay is not established here: the two interventions meant to test
it do not. A companion institutional optimum exists only in a configuration that
does not respond to the market. Five seeds carry the horizon, sweep and
institutional results and twenty carry the shipped-horizon ones; nothing is
calibrated.
\end{abstract}
